title: Any authenticated user can read another customer's order
description: The order detail endpoint calls get_order(), which looks up only by order ID. Unlike the cancellation and return endpoints, it never calls own_order() or otherwise checks customer_id against the authenticated user.
evidence: With a token for Priya (user 1), GET /orders/3 returned Tom's order, including items, prices, payment amount, status, and refunds, with HTTP 200. The vulnerable path is show_order() -> get_order(); own_order() is defined immediately below but is not used here.

title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses the staff check
description: The global admin guard compares request.path to the set of exact URL rules. The refund route is registered with strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler even though the rule set contains /admin/refunds and the guard does not run for the slash variant.
evidence: POST /admin/refunds/ without Authorization and with {"order_id":3,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and created a refund. The canonical POST /admin/refunds without credentials returned HTTP 403. The route is shopapi/admin.py:52-67.

title: Product search is SQL-injectable
description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQLite LIKE expression instead of being passed as a parameter. An unauthenticated caller can alter the WHERE clause and potentially use database-specific SQL injection techniques.
evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all six products (HTTP 200), despite the search term not matching product names. The query is built by string concatenation at shopapi/products.py:40-42.

title: Review bodies are stored and rendered as executable HTML
description: Review body input is inserted into the database without HTML sanitization and product.html renders it with the Jinja safe filter. A customer can persist script or other active markup that executes for every visitor to the product page.
evidence: POST /products/1/reviews as an authenticated customer with {"rating":5,"body":"<script>alert(39889)</script>"} returned 201. GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained the exact payload in <div class="review-body">. The sink is shopapi/templates/product.html:13.

title: The client-controlled basket cookie is unsafe Python pickle data
description: read_basket() base64-decodes and unpickles a cookie supplied by the requester. Pickle deserialization executes reducer callables during loading, so a crafted basket cookie can execute arbitrary code in the web process before the result is type-checked. The cookie is neither signed nor authenticated.
evidence: The attacker-controlled value is read from request.cookies at shopapi/basket.py:16 and passed directly to pickle.loads at line 20; the only validation occurs after deserialization at line 23. /basket and /basket/items both invoke read_basket(), making this a remotely reachable code-execution path.

title: A hardcoded JWT signing key permits staff-token forgery
description: The application uses a fixed source-controlled SECRET_KEY to sign and validate all JWTs. Anyone who obtains the source or a deployed copy can mint a token for the existing staff user and access every admin endpoint.
evidence: Using the literal key hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d from config.py, I minted an HS256 token with sub=3 and sent it to GET /admin/users; the running app returned HTTP 200 with the user list. Validation is in shopapi/auth.py:42-45 and admin authorization trusts the loaded user's staff role at shopapi/__init__.py:38-41.

title: Token refresh accepts unsigned, expired, or attacker-modified JWT claims
description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables signature verification and does not require a valid expiration. It uses the untrusted sub claim to load an account and issues a fresh signed token for that account, allowing anyone to impersonate any known user ID.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with an unsigned JWT containing {"sub":1,"exp":9999999999} and an arbitrary signature returned HTTP 200 and a new signed token for user 1. The vulnerable decode is shopapi/auth.py:101-104.

title: Payment-status timeouts fail open as successful payments
description: When the provider status request times out, the handler sets status to paid and moves the order to processing with paid_pence equal to the order total. A transient provider outage therefore lets an order proceed without payment confirmation.
evidence: confirm_payment() catches requests.Timeout at shopapi/payments.py:39-42 and then executes the paid transition at lines 43-45. The comment confirms this is an intentional timeout path; it does not leave the order awaiting reconciliation or require a later positive confirmation.

title: Payment webhook uses a predictable default secret and does not authenticate the amount
description: If WEBHOOK_SECRET is not configured, the application uses the source-visible value whsec-local. In addition, the signature covers only order_id, while status and amount_pence are accepted from the unsigned JSON body. Anyone able to use the default can mark an unpaid order paid for an arbitrary amount, including more than the order total.
evidence: config.py:8 defines WEBHOOK_SECRET with default whsec-local. I generated HMAC-SHA256 over the order ID using that value and POSTed /webhooks/payments with status=paid and amount_pence=999999; the running app accepted the request with HTTP 200. The signature input is only str(order_id) at shopapi/payments.py:53-55, while amount_pence is taken directly at lines 69-71.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted SHA-256 digests
description: User passwords are hashed with a single unsalted SHA-256 operation. Database compromise therefore permits fast dictionary and brute-force cracking, especially because the seed credentials demonstrate that ordinary passwords are accepted.
evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() at shopapi/auth.py:15-16, and the result is stored directly at registration and reset (lines 77-78 and 158-159). There is no per-password salt or work factor such as Argon2, scrypt, or bcrypt.
